newsitem.title: USA: D.C.'s control board chief slams city management.
newsitem.headline: D.C.'s control board chief slams city management.

text.p: District of Columbia's financial control board chief on Tuesday slammed the quality of the city's management and said his panel will announce additional revamping of city personnel soon.

Andrew Brimmer, who was confirmed by Congress as chairman of the city's new five-member control board in 1995, also said the panel has accelerated the due date for a key study on the future of the city's governance structure to June 30 from Sept 30.
Consultants hired by the control board are examining whether D.C.'s current governance structure -- a strong mayor and less powerful city council -- should be revamped.
One option under review is whether D.C. should have a strong, non-elected city manager and a less powerful mayor and city council.
Brimmer said once the panel gets the consultants' study, it will send recommendations to Capitol Hill "soon after."

Brimmer was one of six panelists at a National Press Club forum that debated the future of the financially troubled city and what role the federal government should play in revamping the nation's capital.
He said most of the city's managers have shown "below average performance." He said his panel has found managers "are not well prepared, not committed" and have a "lack of accountability."
Mayor Barry shot back that Brimmer has "gone too far" in his analysis of management. He said he would put D.C. managers up "against any city or county in America."

Panelists included Brimmer; D.C. Mayor Marion Barry; D.C. Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton; U.S. Rep. Tom Davis, R-Va., chairman of the House Government Reform Committee's subpanel on D.C.; Brookings Institution researcher Carol O'Cleireacain; and Carol Thompson Cole, President Clinton's adviser on D.C.
Most speakers, including Rep. Davis, said they oppose President Clinton's call in his recent D.C. revitalization plan for total repeal of the annual federal payment in-lieu-of-taxes for the city.
Davis would not give a figure, but he said an annual payment from Congress should be "significant."

Brimmer noted that the control board began aggressively pushing the city to cut back its workforce in 1996. Those actions are a "forerunner of the kind of action you should see" in the future, he said.
